title: The Blue Slides Called Green
text:
Research on conformity, like Asch's, showed how the majority sways the individual. In Paris in the late 1960s, Serge Moscovici, with Elisabeth Lage and Martine Naffrechoux, reversed the question: can a minority sway the majority?

They brought groups of six women into a lab for what was presented as a study of color perception. After checking that everyone had normal color vision, they showed a series of slides that were clearly blue, varying only in brightness. Each participant said aloud what color she saw. Two of the six were confederates.

In one condition, the two confederates consistently called every slide green. In another, they said green on most slides but blue on the rest. In a control condition, there were no confederates.

In the control groups, almost no one ever said green. With a consistent minority, about 8 percent of the majority's answers were green, and roughly a third of participants said green at least once. With an inconsistent minority, the effect almost vanished. In later tests, participants exposed to the consistent minority were also more likely to see ambiguous blue-green colors as green, suggesting that the minority had shifted perception, not only public answers.
lesson: A lone dissenter can move a group, but only by being consistent and clear over time. If you are in the minority, hold your position steadily rather than wavering.
people: Serge Moscovici, Elisabeth Lage, Martine Naffrechoux
source: Moscovici, S., Lage, E., and Naffrechoux, M. (1969). Influence of a consistent minority on the responses of a majority in a color perception task. Sociometry, 32(4), 365-380.
